title: Functionalism and Neofunctionalism

cards.b:
Realists say states grab for power. Functionalists say: let them build things together instead.

Functionalism argues that peace grows from cooperation in practical, technical tasks such as post, health, transport and trade. As people see the benefits, they trust each other and a web of ties forms. Politics gets pushed to the side.

Neofunctionalism adds politics. It explains how the European Union began and why it deepened.

This topic links directly to the next unit on regional groupings (EU, ASEAN, SAARC). Exam questions ask you to explain "spillover", to compare functionalism with federalism, to test neofunctionalism on the EU, and to contrast it with intergovernmentalism.

It also underpins how we think about the UN's specialised agencies. Know Mitrany, Haas, the Schuman Declaration and the EU treaties in order.

David Mitrany, a Romanian-born British scholar, wrote A Working Peace System (1943), in the middle of the Second World War.

He was unhappy with both the League model of a grand political organisation and with world federation. Borders are political. Needs are technical. So build bodies around functions.

Mitrany's key ideas

  • Form follows function. Create an agency to handle a specific job, whatever its borders. Rivers, health and airlines cross frontiers.
  • Ramification. Success in one area leads people to want cooperation in the next. Habits of cooperation spread.
  • Technocrats over politicians. Experts, not diplomats, should run these bodies.
  • Welfare over sovereignty. Loyalty will shift to bodies that deliver.
  • No need for a single world state.

Models: the Universal Postal Union, the International Telecommunication Union and the ILO. Mitrany's thinking lies behind the idea of UN specialised agencies.

Ernst Haas, a German-American scholar, wrote The Uniting of Europe: Political, Social, and Economic Forces, 1950-1957 (1958). Leon Lindberg (The Political Dynamics of European Economic Integration, 1963) and Philippe Schmitter built on it.

Neofunctionalists kept the idea that cooperation grows step by step, but added three changes.

  • Integration is a political process, driven by interest groups, parties and supranational officials.
  • The key concept is spillover.
  • Elites shift their loyalty and expectations to a new centre.

Haas defined integration as a process in which actors in several national settings are persuaded to shift their loyalties, expectations and political activities toward a new centre whose institutions have jurisdiction over the existing states.

Where Mitrany wanted to avoid politics, Haas put politics at the centre. The European Coal and Steel Community was the model.

Haas and Lindberg described three kinds of spillover.

  • Functional: integrating one sector creates problems that need integration of related sectors. A common market needs common standards and then a common currency.
  • Political: interest groups and parties turn to the European level, because that is where decisions are made.
  • Cultivated: supranational institutions, such as the Commission, push the process along. Jean Monnet's method is the model.

• 9 May 1950: Robert Schuman, French foreign minister (inspired by Jean Monnet), proposes pooling coal and steel. This is the Schuman Declaration, still celebrated as Europe Day.
  • 1951: Treaty of Paris creates the ECSC (France, West Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, Luxembourg). In force 1952.
  • 1957: Treaties of Rome set up the EEC and Euratom (in force 1958).
  • 1965-66: De Gaulle's "empty chair" crisis. The Luxembourg Compromise (1966) kept a national veto on vital interests.
  • 1986-87: Single European Act: single market by 1992.
  • 1992-93: Maastricht Treaty makes the European Union, with plans for the euro.
  • 1999-2002: Euro launched, with notes in 2002.
  • 2007-09: Lisbon Treaty.
  • 2020: UK leaves (Brexit).
  • 2026: Bulgaria joins the euro on 1 January, as its 21st member. The EU has 27 members.

This path, steady and sectoral, looked like neofunctionalism.

De Gaulle's veto of British entry (1963 and 1967) and the empty chair crisis (1965) shook neofunctionalism.

Stanley Hoffmann, in "Obstinate or Obsolete? The Fate of the Nation-State and the Case of Western Europe" (1966), made the main challenge. He drew a line between "low politics" (economy, welfare) and "high politics" (defence, foreign policy, identity). States will cooperate on the first, but guard the second. Spillover stops at high politics. This became intergovernmentalism.

Haas himself wrote "The Obsolescence of Regional Integration Theory" (1975), admitting that the theory did not fit.

Other critiques:

  • It was Eurocentric. Attempts in Africa, Latin America and South Asia did not follow the pattern.
  • It underrates outside shocks, such as the Cold War and the US role.
  • It assumes integration is a one-way ratchet. Brexit reversed it.

Liberal intergovernmentalism

Andrew Moravcsik, The Choice for Europe (1998). Integration is the result of bargains between governments. National leaders respond to domestic business and farm interests, bargain with each other, and set up institutions to keep promises credible. The EU is a tool of states. Not an independent force.

Supranational governance

Alec Stone Sweet and Wayne Sandholtz (1998): rising cross-border exchange creates demand for rules, and the European Court of Justice and the Commission respond. This revives neofunctionalism.

Others

Karl Deutsch, Political Community and the North Atlantic Area (1957): a security community arises through dense communication and transactions. Constructivists study how European identity forms. Federalists, such as Altiero Spinelli, want a European federation.

Neofunctionalism returned after the euro crisis (2010-12) and Brexit as scholars debated "failing forward".

Students often mix these up. Here is the contrast in plain terms.

Functionalism

Cooperate on technical tasks. Skip big politics. Peace comes from below. No world government.

Neofunctionalism

Same step-by-step logic, but led by elites and institutions. Politics matters. Spillover pushes toward a supranational centre.

Federalism

Make a constitutional union at once, with a central government. Peace comes from above. Examples: Spinelli, Kant's federation.

Realism and intergovernmentalism

States guard sovereignty. Cooperation reflects state interests. Integration stops at high politics.

The Monnet method is functionalist in spirit. The aim was political (a federation) while the route was economic.

Functionalist logic appeals to South Asia, where political quarrels block grand projects.

  • SAARC (founded in Dhaka, 1985) began with "integrated programmes of action" in agriculture, health, telecom, and rural development. SAFTA (signed 2004, in force 2006) followed. But political disputes froze the group; its last summit was in Kathmandu in 2014.
  • BIMSTEC (1997) works through sectors: transport, energy, trade, fisheries.
  • International Solar Alliance (2015) is a functional body on one technical issue.
  • The BBIN Motor Vehicles Agreement (2015) tried to connect Bangladesh, Bhutan, India and Nepal by road.

The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) is a famous functional success: it survived wars. But in April 2025 India put it in abeyance after the Pahalgam attack. Pakistan says it stays in force, and a Court of Arbitration said in August 2026 that it does. India rejects that ruling. It shows the limit: spillover fails when high politics intrudes, as Hoffmann said.

"Explain the functionalist and neofunctionalist approaches to international integration."
"What is spillover? Is it a useful concept to understand regional integration?"
"Compare functionalism with federalism."
"Neofunctionalism is not able to explain the setbacks to European integration." Discuss.

Structure: define functionalism (Mitrany, 1943: form follows function, ramification). Then neofunctionalism (Haas, 1958: spillover types, elites, supranational bodies). Apply to the EU timeline with 4-5 dates. Critique: Hoffmann's high versus low politics, Moravcsik's intergovernmentalism, Brexit. Conclude with South Asia: SAARC, BIMSTEC, Indus Waters Treaty.

Draw the spillover chain. It is quick and scores well.

quiz.w: Agencies should be shaped by the task, not by borders.

quiz.q: Who wrote The Uniting of Europe (1958)?

quiz.w: The Commission and similar bodies actively promote further integration.

quiz.q: The Schuman Declaration was made on:
quiz.w: 9 May 1950, now celebrated as Europe Day.

quiz.q: The Luxembourg Compromise (1966) ended the crisis caused by:
quiz.w: France boycotted from 1965; the compromise protected vital national interests through a veto.
High politics (defence, identity) is where states hold the line.

quiz.q: Karl Deutsch's Political Community and the North Atlantic Area (1957) introduced the idea of:
quiz.w: A security community is a group where war has become unthinkable.

quiz.q: Which treaty created the European Coal and Steel Community?
quiz.w: Signed in Paris in 1951, in force from 1952.
